questions.question_text: What percentage of elderly patients with delirium will go on to develop dementia?
questions.explanation: Among the elderly 10 -15% of patients have delirium on admission, and a further 10 -40% develop delirium during their hospital stay. Liposwski (1983) reported no detectable cause for delirium in between 5 and 20% of cases.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of dementia in the general population older than 65 years of age is approximately
questions.explanation: As the population grows older, the prevalence of dementia is increasing. Moderate to severe dementia is seen in approximately 5% of the general population older than 65 years of age, 20 to 40% in the general population older than 85 years. Dementia of the Alzheimer's type (Alzheimer's disease) is the most common affecting 2/3rds of all patients with dementia.

questions.question_text: In old age, what percentage of patients visit their General Practitioner a week before suicide?
questions.explanation: Approximately two-thirds of individuals who commit suicide have visited their physicians within one month before taking their lives; 40 to 50 percent have visited the week before.

questions.question_text: The risk of vascular events in the elderly increases with use of atypical antipsychotics by a factor of
questions.explanation: Having reviewed the literature on the use of risperidone and olanzapine for the treatment of behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia, the chairman of the CSM concluded that each was associated with at least a two-fold increase in the risk of stroke and therefore should no longer be used in dementia (Duff, 2004; Herrmann et al., 2004; Retrieved from Karim & Byrne, http://apt.rcpsych.org/content/aptrcpsych/11/4/286.full.pdf). 'Health Canada and the FDA issued public warnings based on their own analysis of data from published and unpublished RCTs showing increased mortality in older adults with dementia receiving atypical antipsychotics (Health Canada 2005a; United States Food and Drug Administration 2005). In their review of 17 RCTs involving risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole, the mortality rate was approximately 1.7 times higher than placebo'. (Excerpt retrieved from http://europepmc.org/articles/PMC2671943/).

questions.question_text: The tau gene is located on chromosome
questions.explanation: The Tau gene is located on chromosome 17q21. The Tau proteins modulate the stability of axonal microtubules.

questions.question_text: In dementia of Alzheimer's type, the gene for Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is found on the long arm of chromosome
questions.explanation: The Beta Amyloid precursor protein gene (Chromosome 21) that is found on the long arm of chromosome 21 handles amyloid deposition seen in Alzheimer's disease. Whether the processing of abnormal Amyloid precursor protein is of primary causative significance in Alzheimer's disease is unknown, but many research groups are studying both the normal metabolic processing of Amyloid precursor protein and its processing in patients with dementia of the Alzheimer's type in an attempt to answer this question.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of paraphrenia in elderly above the age of 65 is
questions.explanation: People with late paraphrenia represent approximately 10% of the elderly population of psychiatric hospitals. The reported prevalence of the disorder among the elderly living in the community ranges from 0.1 to 4%, and its incidence has been estimated to be between 10 -26 per 100 000 per year. (Almeida, O. P., Howard, R., Forstl, H., et al. (1992) Late paraphrenia: a review. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, 7, 543 - 548.)

questions.question_text: In elderly patients, what is the ideal target serum therapeutic level of lithium that is required for the treatment of mania?
questions.explanation: A lower therapeutic range around 0.4 to 0.6mmol/L is suggested for prophylaxis in the elderly with bipolar disorder (Shulman, 2002). Age appropriate doses of neuroleptics may also be used.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of clinical depression in community samples over age 65 is
questions.explanation: Community samples show a higher prevalence of depression especially in the elderly. In specific settings such as residential care homes, the prevalence may be still higher.

questions.question_text: In the population aged over 65 the overall prevalence of clinically significant depression is estimated at
questions.explanation: In the population aged over 65 the prevalence of clinically significant depression is 10%. This figure is increased in hospital subpopulations and higher still in residential homes (Fountaulakis et al. 2003). Residential and nursing homes have a prevalence of 15 -30%.

questions.question_text: The proportion of patients with dementia in whom the condition is attributable to vascular causes is given by
questions.explanation: Dementia from all causes has a prevalence of about 8% over the age of 65. Roughly 10 -40% of these cases are vascular, with distribution differing regionally. An additional one -third may have mixed vascular and Alzheimer's pathology. 'The proportion of cases due to VaD falls with increasing age but even so, the prevalence of all dementia rises so rapidly with age that the prevalence of VaD also rises. Males are more commonly affected than females' (Retrieved from http://jnnp.bmj.com/content/76/suppl_5/v35.full.pdf).

questions.question_text: The estimated proportion of acute confusional states that develop during hospitalisation that are considered preventable is given by
questions.explanation: An estimated 30 -40% of cases of delirium are preventable and prevention is the most effective strategy for minimizing the occurrence of delirium and its adverse outcomes. Drugs such as benzodiazepines or anticholinergics and other known precipitants of delirium should be avoided. Also, benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal is a common preventable cause of delirium (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3065676/).

questions.question_text: The 10 -year probability of conversion from Mild Cognitive Impairment to dementia is
questions.explanation: Mitchell and Shiri -Feshki (2009) conducted a meta-analysis of 41 high -quality studies and noted that the yearly conversion rate from MCI to dementia is around 5 -10%; even after 10 years, only 40% (not the majority) of MCI patients will progress to dementia. Other meta -analyses of long -term (5 -10 years) studies present still lower yearly conversion rates, varying between 3.3 – 4.2%, with cumulative conversion rates of ~31% over ten years (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19236314).

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old gentleman has been diagnosed with amnestic -MCI (Mild cognitive impairment). What is the likelihood of him developing Alzheimer's dementia in a year's time?
questions.explanation: Studies suggest that individuals with MCI tend to progress to probable Alzheimer's disease at a rate of approximately 10% per year.

questions.question_text: A 79-year-old lady was admitted to the psychiatric ward with a history of paranoid psychosis and has been started on chlorpromazine. How high is the risk of this lady suffering from tardive dyskinesia compared to a 33 -year-old lady treated for the same condition with the same dose?
questions.explanation: The risk of developing Tardive dyskinesia with older antipsychotics is increased in older people by 5 -6 times (Kane 1999).

questions.question_text: What is the average life expectancy of patients diagnosed with Lewy body dementia?
questions.explanation: People with Lewy body dementia have an average life expectancy of about six years after diagnosis. Lobo A, Launer LJ, Fratiglioni L et al. (2000) Prevalence of dementia and major subtypes in Europe: A collaborative study of population -based cohorts. Neurology 54: S4, S9.

questions.question_text: Very late onset schizophrenia is characterised by onset after;
questions.explanation: The late-onset psychotic illness is further subdivided into late onset (onset after 40 years of age) and very late onset (onset after 60 years of age). The prevalence of schizophrenia (early, late and very late onset combined) in the elderly (>65 years) is around 1%. (Cohen et al. 2000).

questions.question_text: Among elderly patients admitted to an intensive care unit, the prevalence of delirium is around
questions.explanation: The overall prevalence of delirium in the community is just 1 -2%, but in the setting of general hospital admission this increases to 14 -24%. The incidence of delirium arising during a hospital stay ranges from 6% to as high as 56%, and this incidence is even higher when more -specialized populations are considered, including those in postoperative, intensive-care, subacute and palliative -care settings. Postoperative delirium occurs in 15 -53% of surgical patients over the age of 65 years, and among elderly patients admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) the delirium incidence can reach 70-87%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with respect to late onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Persecutory delusions are the most common symptoms of late paraphrenia; they are found in around 90% of patients (Almeida et al., 1995a). Auditory hallucinations occur in approximately 75% of cases.

questions.question_text: Characteristic features of very late onset schizophrenia would include all except

options.text: A lower likelihood of family history of schizophrenia
A greater likelihood of visual hallucinations
A lower likelihood of affective blunting
A greater risk of developing Tardive dyskinesia
A greater likelihood of formal thought disorder

correct_answer.text: A greater likelihood of formal thought disorder

correct_answers.text: A greater likelihood of formal thought disorder

questions.explanation: Characteristic features of very late onset schizophrenia include a significantly higher number of females being affected than males and a lower chance of observing formal thought disorder, affective blunting and a higher chance of Tardive dyskinesia.

questions.question_text: According to the UK National Psychiatric Morbidity Survey, the factor NOT associated with the risk of a neurotic disorder is
questions.explanation: Age 55 -64 is not associated with the risk of a neurotic disorder.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 76 -year-old gentleman in the memory clinic. On routine blood tests, his calcium levels are noted to be high. Low levels of which of the following can artificially elevate calcium in the blood?
questions.explanation: The amount of total calcium varies with the level of serum albumin, a protein to which calcium is bound. So when albumin levels are low, free calcium levels will be high in the plasma as they are not bound to proteins. Therefore low levels of albumin can artificially elevate calcium levels in the blood. Low albumin levels (hypoalbuminaemia) may be caused by various conditions such as liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, malabsorption, malnutrition (common in older people with dementia), burns, late pregnancy, artefact, genetic variations and malignancy.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a recognized finding in a normal ageing brain?

options.text: Tau proteins in some nerve cells
Lipofuscin in the cytoplasm of nerve cells
Lewy bodies in substantia nigra and locus cereleus
Hirano bodies in new hippocambal pyramidal cells

questions.explanation: Other possible expected changes in old age include the appearance of senile plaques in the neocortex, amygdala, hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.

questions.question_text: Factors contributing to an increased risk of psychosis in the elderly would include

options.text: Age related deterioration of frontal and temporal cortices
Age related Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties

questions.explanation: The contributory factors for increased risk of psychosis in elderly people would include; Neurochemical changes associated with ageing, age -related deterioration of frontal and temporal cortices, cognitive decline, social isolation, sensory deprivation, age -related Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties, use of polypharmacy, etc.

questions.question_text: All are true about delirium in palliative care except

options.text: occurs in over 50% of patients at some stage in their illness

questions.explanation: Delirium in palliative care is often multifactorial, and causes are often not ascertained accurately. Though some response to neuroleptics can be expected, it does not happen always. It is very common in palliative setting; in one case series, more than 50 % of patients in palliative care had either hypoactive (common) or hyperactive variant of delirium. Dein, S. Psychiatric liaison in palliative care. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment (2003) 9: 241 -248.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man reports hearing 'burglar noises' in his attic every night. He believes that his neighbours are spying on him and are planning a 'coup' to evacuate him from his bungalow. He seems depressed due to this problem but has no somatic signs. The most likely cause of such a late -onset psychosis is
questions.explanation: The most common cause of late onset psychosis is Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for psychiatric disorders in the elderly?

options.text: feeling a burden on the family
inadequately controlled physical symptoms, especially pain

questions.explanation: Uncertain, ambivalent religious beliefs are indicated as risk factors for psychiatric morbidity in the elderly (CR104: RCPsych).

questions.question_text: Which of the following drug interacts with lithium and reduces its serum levels?
questions.explanation: Aminophylline increases lithium excretion and reduces serum lithium levels. Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as Indomethacin, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin two antagonists, fluoxetine can reduce the renal clearance of lithium and, therefore, increases serum lithium levels in the blood.

questions.question_text: Which of the following personality traits is associated with suicide in people aged over 60 years?
questions.explanation: A case-control study using retrospective information of personality traits showed that anankastic and anxious personality disorders are predictors of suicide in older people. (Harwood et al. 2001).

questions.question_text: The personality disorder most commonly associated with suicide in those over the age 60 is
questions.explanation: According to a study by Harwood et al., among older subjects who committed suicide, 77% had a psychiatric disorder at the time of death, most often depression (63%). Personality disorder or personality trait accentuation was present in 44%, with anankastic or anxious traits being the most frequent. (Retrieved from Psychiatric disorder and personality factors associated with suicide in older people: a descriptive and case-control study. Harwood et al., http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following feature is seen more in the cortical type of dementia than the subcortical type?
questions.explanation: Features of cortical dementias include early aphasia, acalculia and significant memory loss in early stages. Examples of cortical dementia include Alzheimer's disease, Picks disease, etc. Subcortical dementias usually have no aphasia and calculation is preserved until late, but speed of cognitive processing is slowed early, along with the appearance of depressed mood, dysarthric speech, slowed motor speed and control, bowed or extended posture, apathetic personality, adventitious movements like tics, chorea, tremors and dystonia. Examples of subcortical dementias include Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, etc.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a proven protective factor in late onset familial dementia of Alzheimer's type?
questions.explanation: Being a carrier of apolipoprotein e2 allele can be a protective factor against the development of Alzheimer's dementia.

questions.question_text: What is the mode of inheritance of Pick's disease?
questions.explanation: A proportion of Pick's disease cases is familial though the majority are sporadic with no other family members being affected. In the familial cases, it is known as an 'autosomal dominant' disease and tends to affect people by about 40 years of age. There is strong family history in 50% of cases. Genetics: Associations with 17q21 -22 (familial inheritance) and mutations in the tau gene.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is widely used to summarize information on activities of daily living in the elderly?

options.text: Clifton assessment procedure for the elderly

questions.explanation: The Barthel index of the activities of daily living (ADL) is a means of assessing the degree of disability in a particular individual, and it helps to communicate patient needs to other health professionals effectively. "The Barthel index records indicators of independence in terms of the disability caused by impairments that give a score out of 20, principally concerned with physical aspects of disability. The Barthel index is at its best when recorded over periods of time by a single individual, a measure of improvement of a patient. A score of 14 indicates some disability, usually compatible with the level of support found in a residential home, a score of 10 compatible with discharge home provided there is maximum support and a carer in attendance"(Retrieved from http://www.gpnotebook.co.uk/simplepage.cfm?ID=429522946).

questions.question_text: Factors associated with late paraphrenia include all, except:
questions.explanation: There is no correlation between educational achievement and paraphrenia. Sensory impairment, being female and social isolation (especially being single) are associated with increased risk of paraphrenia.

questions.question_text: An elderly patient presented with anxiety and insomnia but became sexually disinhibited after taking a newly prescribed medication. What is the likely medication?
questions.explanation: Side effects of BDZs in elderly: Induce dependence potential; can increase the risk of falls and disinhibition in the elderly.

questions.question_text: A patient had a large haemorrhagic stroke that fully resolved with treatment two years ago. He later developed vascular dementia after this event. The most likely neurological deficit that can be seen currently is
questions.explanation: A median number of 4.5 signs per patient were noted in a large cohort of vascular dementia patients. Reflex asymmetry was the most prevalent symptom (49%) irrespective of the extent of vascular insult. Measures of small vessel disease were associated with an increased prevalence of dysarthria, dysphagia, parkinsonian gait disorder, rigidity, and hypokinesia and as well to hemimotor dysfunction. By contrast, in the presence of a cerebral infarct, aphasia, reflex asymmetry, hemianopia, hemimotor dysfunction, hemisensory dysfunction, and hemiplegic gait disorder were more often observed. Staekenborg, S. S., van der Flier, W. M., van Straaten, E. C. W., et al. (2008) Neurological Signs in Relation to Type of Cerebrovascular Disease in Vascular Dementia. Stroke, 39, 317 -322.

questions.question_text: The most common cause of death in patients with dementia of Alzheimer's type is
questions.explanation: Dysphagia and aspiration pneumonia are the two most serious medical conditions seen in late-stage Alzheimer's disease. Pseudobulbar dysphagia is associated with weight loss, which is not always prevented by optimizing the management of the dysphagia. Failure of basic homeostatic mechanisms appears to play an important role in the nutritional status of these patients. Aspiration pneumonia is the most common cause of death in end-stage dementia. (Kalla 2003).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is used for the differential diagnosis of cognitive dysfunction in older people?
questions.explanation: The Cambridge examination for mental disorders, also called CAMDEX -R, gives operational criteria which it suggests are used for clinical diagnosis and guidelines for classifying dementia, according to clinical severity. It enables to make a differential diagnosis of dementia to be made according to the most recent criteria. It comprises of a structured clinical interview; a brief neuropsychological battery; a structured interview with a relative; the diagnostic criteria from DSM-IV and ICD-10 for dementia and other categories including differential with depression (Retrieved from http://pb.rcpsych.org/content/24/5/199.2).

questions.question_text: Which scale is useful to obtain a differential diagnosis of dementia among the elderly?
questions.explanation: The CAMDEX incorporates MMSE, Blessed dementia rating scale and Haschinski Ischemia score, in a comprehensive inquiry from the subject and informant. BDRS is a measure of activities of daily living. The Hachinski Ischemia Score helps to differentiate between vascular and Alzheimer's dementia. A notable feature of CAMDEX is CAMCOG, which is the cognitive subscale. Trained non-doctors mainly use CAMDEX in research. (Seminars in old age psychiatry -14).

questions.question_text: Mr. Z is a 75 -year-old gentleman seen at the psychogeriatric clinic for cognitive and language difficulties. His speech is characterised by distinctive slurring of consonants accompanied by a staccato pattern. Which of the following disorders is most likely to account for this type of presentation?
questions.explanation: Staccato or scanning speech with poor modulation of the volume and pitch of the speech is seen in cerebellar disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is not required for a probable diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease according to the NINCDS/ADRDA Criteria? (National institute of neurological and communicative disorders and stroke/Alzheimer's disease and Related disorders association)

options.text: Cerebral atrophy on a CT head scan
Abnormal cognitive function on formal testing
An absence of other disorders causing dementia

correct_answer.text: Cerebral atrophy on a CT head scan

correct_answers.text: Cerebral atrophy on a CT head scan

questions.explanation: According to NINCDS -ADRDA criteria proposed in 1984, for a probable Alzheimer's disease, dementia should be established by clinical and neuropsychological examination. Cognitive impairments also have to be progressive and be present in 2 or more areas of cognition. The onset of the deficits has been between the ages of 40 and 90 years and finally there must be an absence of other diseases capable of producing a dementia syndrome. For a definite diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, the patient should meet the criteria for probable Alzheimer's disease with histopathologic evidence of Alzheimer's disease (autopsy).

questions.question_text: Which of the following scales includes an assessment of the activities of daily living?
questions.explanation: The CDR score is derived from a standard set of information collected in a clinical instrument that uses other popular scales - for example, the collateral source or informant interview incorporates much of the Blessed Dementia Scale. Other specific ADL scales include Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ) Cleveland Scale of Activities of Daily Living (CSADL) Direct Assessment of Functional Status (DAFS), Bristol Activities of Daily Living Scale (BADLS) etc. AGECAT is a computerised diagnostic system for use with the Geriatric Mental State (GMS), a semi-structured interview for use with older people. It provides syndrome diagnoses of organicity, schizophrenia, mania, depression, anxiety, obsessional disorder, phobia, and hypochondriasis. It then provides a differential diagnosis. Used in conjunction with the History and Aetiology Schedule it provides subtyping of dementia.

questions.question_text: All of the following features correlate with the severity of Alzheimer's dementia except

options.text: Declining Mini Mental state examination scores
Neurological features such as seizures and myoclonus
Declining activities of daily living scores

questions.explanation: Depression is seen across varying severities of dementia, but may be more common or clinically evident in those with mild to moderate dementia.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old gentleman presents with a 3 -year history of memory and language difficulties. Which of the following neurological findings would make a diagnosis of previous cerebrovascular disease more likely?

options.text: Facial weakness with inability to raise eyebrows
Diminished power of the lower limbs
Muscle wasting of lower left leg

questions.explanation: Clonus is an alternating flexion and extension of the foot, which may be spontaneous or induced by rapidly dorsiflexing the foot and holding in that position by slight pressure. The lesion is most likely in the pyramidal tract, and CT/MRI scan of the brain findings may suggest cerebrovascular disease, space occupying lesion or multiple sclerosis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false with respect to personality disorders in old age?

options.text: Cluster B disorders are the most common
Personality disorders can be diagnosed after the age of 65
Rates of personality disorders is highest among those with depression
Diogenes syndrome is considered as an end -stage of personality disorder
Personality disorders contribute to treatment resistance in depression

correct_answer.text: Cluster B disorders are the most common

correct_answers.text: Cluster B disorders are the most common

questions.explanation: The diagnostic criteria for personality disorders are somewhat age-biased as they require evidence of dysfunction from younger ages - this information may not be available when diagnosing personality disorders in elderly for the first time. Nevertheless, there is no restriction for making such diagnoses in the elderly. No specific cluster differences are noted in the prevalence rates of personality disorders in the elderly though a lower prevalence of cluster B is suggested.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a subcortical type of dementia?
questions.explanation: Subcortical dementias usually have no aphasia and calculation is preserved until late, but speed of cognitive processing is slowed early, along with the appearance of depressed mood, dysarthric speech, slowed motor speed and control, bowed or extended posture, apathetic personality, adventitious movements like tics, chorea, tremors and dystonia. Examples of subcortical dementias include Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, etc. CJD is multifocal dementia affecting cerebral cortex and cerebellum along with subcortical structures.

questions.question_text: Periodic complexes in EEG is a feature seen in
questions.explanation: EEG shows periodic complexes; periodic bi or triphasic discharges against slight low voltage background Is seen in the dementia of Creutzfeldt -Jakob disease.

questions.question_text: Abrupt onset and fluctuating course are typical and highly suggestive of
questions.explanation: Clinical features of delirium include a rapid onset of clinical features with fluctuations in severity over minutes and hours (even back to apparent normality).

questions.question_text: An 85 -year-old gentleman was admitted to a medical ward with a history of distressing visual hallucinations for the last 2 days. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Delirium: Onset of clinical features is rapid with fluctuations in severity over minutes and hours (with periods of apparent normality). Features include clouding of consciousness with reduced attention span and distractibility, global impairment of cognition with disorientation, and impairment of recent memory and abstract thinking, disturbance in sleep/wake cycle with nocturnal worsening of symptoms, psychomotor agitation and emotional lability, perceptual distortions, illusions, and hallucinations (characteristically visual) along with a rambling, incoherent, and thought disordered speech. There may be poorly developed paranoid delusions.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following scales used in delirium has good symptom coverage and distinguishes delirium from other disorders?
questions.explanation: The delirium rating scale is the most widely used, but it needs interpretation by a skilled clinician or information from multiple clinical sources. It has the advantage of distinguishing delirium from dementia. MMSE emphasizes neuropsychological functions linked to the dominant cerebral hemisphere. But several core disturbances of delirium such as attention reflect non-dominant or non-localized hemispheric functions. The cognitive test for delirium (CTD) allows detailed investigation of a range of neuropsychological functions such as orientation, comprehension, attention and memory and is suitable for use in patients with impaired communication due to immobility, intubation or absence of verbal abilities. The CAM (Confusion assessment method) has high sensitivity and specificity, which allows a diagnosis of delirium and is readily incorporated in routine clinical settings. It has reduced sensitivity when used by nursing staff rather than physicians (Meagherand MacDonald, 2001).

questions.question_text: In people with Alzheimer's disease, the most common psychotic symptoms are
questions.explanation: The prevalence of psychosis in people with Alzheimer's disease ranges between 30 and 50%. Delusions were more common than hallucinations (Bassiony et al. 2000) Visual and auditory hallucinations are more common Although hallucinations can occur in all modalities. (Tariot 1995). There is some evidence of the association of psychotic symptoms with a rapid decline in cognition in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following syndromes is considered to be an end stage of personality disorder in older people?
questions.explanation: Diogenes syndrome: Also called 'senile squalor syndrome' refers to a syndrome of self-neglect in older people, in which eccentric and reclusive individuals become increasingly isolated and neglect themselves, living in filthy, poor conditions. It can be seen as the response of someone with a particular personality type to the hardships of old age and loneliness (Howard and Bergman 1993) and is considered to be a end stage of personality disorder in older people.

questions.question_text: An 83 -year-old woman presents with memory loss, confusion and disorientation. Which of the following features is most suggestive of a delirium?
questions.explanation: Disturbance of sleep-wake cycle is one of the core symptoms suggestive of delirium. The delirium is usually acute in onset and consciousness is clouded with decreased attention span and distractibility.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most common in delirium?
questions.explanation: Clinical symptoms and signs of delirium include impairment of consciousness; thinking; memory; psychomotor behaviour; perception; and emotion. The onset is often rapid and the course is diurnally fluctuating, usually lasting less than six months. EEG usually but not invariably shows a slowing of the background activity. Impairment of consciousness characteristically fluctuates often, with deterioration in the evening. Characteristically, in delirium tremens a hyper alert state is seen, with the patient attending to all external stimuli without discrimination. A minor degree of impaired consciousness manifests as difficulty in estimating the passage of time. This is tested by asking the patient to estimate how long the interview/hospital stay has lasted. The sleep/wake cycle is almost always (nearly 98% in a study) disturbed, with marked periods of drowsiness, sleep in the day, and insomnia at night. The prevalence of psychotic symptoms in a retrospective chart review of >800 patients showed that the prevalence of psychotic symptoms was 42.7% with 27% of patients having visual hallucinations, 12.4% having auditory hallucinations, 2.7% having tactile hallucinations, and 25.6% having delusions. Burns, A et al. Delirium. Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery and Psychiatry 2004; 75:362 -367. Webster R and Holroyd S. Prevalence of psychotic symptoms in delirium.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scale is useful in the assessment of Alzheimer's disease among the learning disabled population?
questions.explanation: MMSE has a floor effect and not useful for screening for dementia in Down's syndrome. NINDS criteria are generalized diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer's disease but not a screening tool adapted for Down's syndrome. The Dementia Questionnaire for Mentally Retarded Persons (DMR) is useful for general screening for Alzheimer's disease among the intellectually disabled.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?

options.text: Memantine is a selective butyrylcholinesterase inhibitor
Galantamine does not act directly on nicotine receptors
Ginkgo biloba has same efficacy as Donepezil
Donepezil is metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4
Tacrine is not used due to risk of pulmonary embolism

correct_answer.text: Donepezil is metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4

correct_answers.text: Donepezil is metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4

questions.explanation: Donepezil is metabolized by CYP2D6, CYP3A4 and undergoes glucuronidation. There are four major metabolites produced, one of which is active. The major metabolite that is produced is 6 -o-desmethyl -donepezil. This is present in 20% of the plasma concentration. Galantamine has direct nicotinic stimulatory action. Tacrine is not used due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. A Cochrane review in 2007 found that the evidence for a benefit of Gingko biloba on cognition in individuals with dementia was not convincing. Several small, short-term randomized trials have had mixed results. Memantine is a NMDA antagonist. Birks J, Grimley EV, Van DM. Ginkgo biloba for cognitive impairment and dementia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2002;(4): CD003120.

questions.question_text: Between the ages of 65 and 85, the prevalence of Alzheimer's disease;
questions.explanation: The risk of Alzheimer's dementia increases with age. The risk is 1% at age 60 years, then it doubles every five years, to become 40% in those aged 85 years.

questions.question_text: In progressive supranuclear palsy which of the following is true?

options.text: Onset is usually in 4th decade of life
Cortical type of dementia is noted
A tendency to fall forwards is seen

questions.explanation: PSP is a differential diagnosis of LBD. The onset is in the sixth decade (range 45 to 75 years) and patients present with difficulty in balance, abrupt falls, slurred speech, dysphagia, and vague changes in personality, sometimes with an apprehensiveness and fretfulness suggestive of an agitated depression. The most common early complaint is unsteadiness of gait and unexplained falling (retropulsion).

questions.question_text: Variant CJD is characterised by an early onset of
questions.explanation: The rise of vCJD followed an epidemic of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle. 'BSE is a prion disease of cows that is thought to have been caused by cattle feeds that contained CNS material from infected cows. The disease in humans affects mainly young men in their 20s and is characterised by early anxiety and depressive symptoms, followed by personality changes, and finally progressive dementia'. Ataxia and myoclonus are prominent, and the typical course is 1 -2 yrs until death. (From Semple & Smyth, Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry).

questions.question_text: A 64-year-old patient presents with progressive memory loss, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. He has a history of head injury of moderate severity in the past. Which of the following regarding his diagnosis is correct?

options.text: Elevated CSF pressure will be noted on lumbar puncture
Enlarged ventricles can be seen on neuroimaging
Cortical type of dementia is most common

correct_answer.text: Enlarged ventricles can be seen on neuroimaging

correct_answers.text: Enlarged ventricles can be seen on neuroimaging

questions.explanation: In classic NPH, a head CT shows a moderate to severe ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cerebral atrophy and includes ballooned frontal horns and enlarged temporal horns without evidence of hippocampal atrophy. A seizure is rare; Babinski is usually absent. Subcortical dementia is more common.

questions.question_text: A 78-year-old man presents with depression for the first time. His wife says that his depression is very different from the recurrent depression experienced by her 44 -year-old son. Which one of the following is a feature seen commonly in early onset depression when compared with late -onset depression?
questions.explanation: Although depression in all ages is associated with some degree of impaired concentration and subjective difficulties with memory, these cognitive deficits seem to occur when first onset is in older age (Holroyd and Duryee 1997). Other cognitive deficits such as episodic memory disturbance and executive dysfunction are also commonly found in depression. Studies also found that individuals with late-onset depression had specific deficits in attention and executive functions (Consistent with frontal lobe dysfunction) whereas those with recurrent early-onset depression exhibited deficits in episodic memory (Rapp et al 2005) which is consistent with temporal lobe dysfunction.

options.text: Impairment has been gradually progressive over a period of some months

questions.explanation: Both dementia and delirium are characterized by global cognitive impairment.

questions.question_text: Which factor is most likely to increase the risk of paraphrenia?
questions.explanation: Female gender is the most important risk. Gender distribution is estimated as 4 to 9 female predominance per male. Women appear to run a greater risk of developing late paraphrenia, especially those who are socially isolated and present with associated hearing impairment. Ref: Psychotic states arising in late life (late paraphrenia). The role of risk factors - OP Almeida, RJ Howard, R Levy and AS David.

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical features is not consistent with an ICD -10 diagnosis of delirium?
questions.explanation: In delirium, there is a global disturbance of cognition and is not focal. Other salient features may include impairment of attention and consciousness, psychomotor disturbances, disturbance of the sleep-wake cycle, emotional disturbances and perceptual distortions such as illusions and hallucinations - most often visual.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests would be required to make a diagnosis of Huntington's disease in a patient without a family history?
questions.explanation: The sporadic appearance of new mutations is not uncommon in the Huntington disease gene. Hence, a genetic test is advised even in those who present without a family history.

questions.question_text: A 69-year-old woman lost her husband recently. Which of the following clinical features would support a diagnosis of depression rather than normal grief reaction in this patient?

options.text: Auditory hallucinations of dead husband's voice

questions.explanation: Irrespective of age, a third of those who lose a spouse meet criteria for major depression in the first month after the death, and half of these remain clinically depressed one year later. However, in normal grief reactions substantial improvement is expected within two months to 6 months, and those who continue to meet criteria for major depression after this period should receive antidepressant or psychotherapy. Suicidal ideas, psychotic symptoms other than pseudohallucinations of widowhood and generalized guilt feelings along with persistent symptoms must suggest a depressive episode requiring intervention.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used as the first choice medication for elderly patients with delirium in a surgical ward?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol has the best recommendation and evidence, even superior to benzodiazepines in the treatment of delirium. It has less anticholinergic and sedating effects than other interventions.

questions.question_text: The similarities between early onset and late onset schizophrenia includes all of the following except
questions.explanation: Late-onset schizophrenia is characterised by (Palmer et al. 2001) fewer negative symptoms, better response to antipsychotics and better neuropsychological performance. But it is similar to the usual onset disease in terms of genetic risk, presence and severity of positive symptoms, early psychosocial maladjustments and subtle brain abnormalities revealed by imaging.
